phonemes.desc: Short alpha with smooth breathing, the simple opening of the word.
Long eta with acute plus rho [ɛ̌ːr] — the pitch peak and the core meaning 'air, mist'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ah-HAYR' — the second syllable is long, pitched high, and ends with a rolled or tapped r.

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *h₂weh₁r- 'air, wind'; cognate with Latin aura and possibly air-related Germanic words

pronunciation.note: Aḗr is Tier 1 because the Greek ἀήρ contains both length (η) and stress (acute) on the same syllable. It is one of the elemental words of Greek philosophy and science.

domains.title: The Lower Air
domains.subtitle: Mist, Atmosphere, Breath of Life
domains.lead: Aḗr is the Greek word for the lower air, the misty atmosphere between earth and the bright aithēr above. For Anaximenes it was the arche, the fundamental substance from which all things arise by rarefaction and condensation.

cards.name: Elemental Air
cards.desc: One of the classical elements; the invisible medium of breath, weather, and life.

cards.name: Anaximenes' Arche
cards.desc: The Milesian philosopher made air the single substance underlying all change.

cards.name: Breath and Soul
cards.desc: Greek pneuma and psyche both connect life to the movement of air.

cards.name: Mist and Cloud
cards.desc: Aēr is not pure sky but the cloudy, breathable layer where mortals live.

mythology.lead: Aḗr has no mythic biography; its story is the history of Greek thought. From Homer to Aristotle, it moves from mere atmosphere to a recognized element of the cosmos.

myths.title: Aēr and Aithēr
myths.text: In Homer, aēr is the lower, misty air where mortals breathe and battle; aithēr is the bright upper air of the gods. The distinction sets up a cosmic hierarchy: the higher the air, the more divine it is.

myths.title: Air as Arche
myths.text: Anaximenes of Miletus (6th c. BCE) proposed that aēr is the arche, the fundamental stuff of the universe. When rarefied, it becomes fire; when condensed, it becomes wind, cloud, water, earth, and stone. This was one of the first monistic physical theories in the West.

myths.title: The Element Between
myths.text: Aristotle made aēr one of the four elements, positioned between fire and water. It is hot and wet, mobile and transparent, the natural place of birds and the medium of sound. His scheme dominated Western science for two millennia.

lore.syncretism: Aḗr entered Latin as aura and aer, and from there into the Romance and Germanic languages (English 'air'). It was identified with the pneuma of Stoic physics and with the Holy Spirit in Christian theology, where 'spirit' and 'breath' share a root. Modern chemistry replaced the four-element theory, but 'air' remains the everyday name for Earth's atmosphere.
lore.culturalLegacy: Aḗr is so ordinary that we forget it is sacred: every breath is a gift of atmosphere. The word survives in 'air,' 'aerial,' 'aerodynamics,' and 'aerospace.' Environmental science now treats air as a global commons, making the ancient element a political and ethical concern. To restore aḗr in Unicode is to name the invisible substance we share.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Aḗr is the element we cannot see but cannot live without. Philosophers made it the source of all things because it is everywhere, changeable, and necessary. We breathe it, speak through it, and move within it; it carries both perfume and plague.

The Milesian insight still resonates: air is not emptiness but substance. Modern physics confirms that the atmosphere is a thin, fragile layer of gases held by gravity. To think of aḗr is to think of commons — what we all need and what we can all harm. The Greek word thus becomes an ecological name, as urgent now as when Anaximenes first called it the arche.

sources.name: Aristotle, On the Heavens and Meteorology

lore.archaeology: Aḗr has no cult sites, but its material trace is atmospheric and technological: ancient wind towers, pneumatic devices described by Hero of Alexandria, and the development of meteorology. The concept shaped Greek architecture, medicine, and philosophy, leaving its mark in texts rather than temples.
